title: Cylinder Defect Casimir Energy and Weyl Anomalies
abstract: We distinguish two Casimir observables associated with a conformal surface defect. A circular cylinder embedded in flat space has a logarithmic contribution to its Casimir energy, $-d_1\log(R/ε)/(24R)$, fixed by the displacement anomaly. A great cylinder obtained by radial quantization of the ambient theory instead has Casimir energy $-b/(12R)$ in the conformal defect vacuum with a fixed local anomaly convention. Free-field and holographic calculations provide checks of the proposed relations in both embeddings.
summary: This paper calculates the Casimir energy associated with defects on curved surfaces, distinguishing between two geometric embeddings: a circular cylinder and a great cylinder. By employing anomaly matching techniques and comparing free-field and holographic results, the authors derive specific energy formulas dependent on geometric parameters and anomaly coefficients. This work provides a detailed theoretical framework for understanding boundary contributions to vacuum energy in quantum field theories.
main_problem: The paper determines the Casimir energy associated with a conformal surface defect, comparing results for two distinct geometric embeddings: a circular cylinder and a great cylinder.
main_result: The Casimir energy for the great cylinder is found to be $E_{	ext{great}} = -b/(12R)$, while the circular cylinder yields $E_{\log} = - rac{d_1}{24R} \log(R/\epsilon)$.
method: The authors employ anomaly matching, utilizing defect Ward identities, free-field calculations, and holographic methods (like Wess–Zumino functionals) to constrain the vacuum energy.
model_or_system: The analysis considers a two-dimensional conformal field theory (CFT) on a circle coupled to a higher-dimensional CFT, exhibiting a conformal surface defect $\Sigma$. Calculations are performed on both bent (circular) and great cylinder geometries.
key_observables: Casimir energy ($E$), defect anomaly coefficients ($d_1, b$), and the Weyl response density ($\mathcal{A}_D$).
important_parameters: Radius $R$, cutoff scale $\epsilon$, and anomaly coefficients $d_1$ and $b$.
main_assumptions: The results rely on specific conventions for anomaly definitions and the careful subtraction of counterterms to handle divergences.

paper_structure: The paper systematically compares the energy calculations for the two embeddings, deriving the logarithmic and inverse-linear energy forms using anomaly constraints, and verifying these results using free-field and holographic models.
why_interesting: The rigorous calculation of boundary/defect energy via anomaly matching provides powerful techniques applicable to open quantum systems and boundary effects in condensed matter models.
